title: A garden plan
text: Our class had an [[idea]]: we could grow plants beside the window. We had no garden, so we used small [[pots]]. We put them near the glass [[because]] the plants needed light.

title: The missing labels
text: There was a problem with our map: some names were [[missing]]. We needed to [[change]] it by adding the names of the roads. We used red for the names, [[but]] we kept the roads black.

title: Water for the plants
text: The chart can [[show]] how much water each plant needs. We check it [[before]] we water the plants. This is [[important]] because too much water can hurt them. The cactus needs less water than the other plants.

title: The class survey
text: We wanted to know which books students liked. We asked a [[question]] about their favourite stories. Animal stories were the most [[popular]] answer. We [[also]] found that many students liked books about space.

title: A good answer
text: Read the question [[before]] you write. If it asks who found the bag, your [[answer]] must give a person's name. It is [[important]] to copy that name correctly. Check it in the text when you finish.

title: A poster in the hall
text: The poster in the hall shows a paper boat on a river. To [[describe]] it, start with what you can see: its colours, pictures and words. The boat is one small [[detail]] in the picture. The poster asks people to keep rivers [[clean]]. Its title is easy to read [[because]] it stands out from the blue background. The words and picture work [[together]] to explain the event.

title: The mystery seed
text: The class grew two plants from the same kind of seed. Maya [[compared]] the plants by measuring their [[height]] each morning. After two weeks, the plant by the window had [[more]] leaves than the plant in the cupboard. The amount of light might help to [[explain]] why. Next time, both plants would receive the [[same]] amount of water.

title: Rainy-day experiment
text: Too little light can [[cause]] a plant to grow slowly. The class moved one plant from a dark cupboard to a sunny window. After two weeks, it had six leaves [[instead of]] three. This was an [[increase]] in the number of leaves. The new leaves were green and [[healthy]]. The class recorded these changes in a [[table]].

title: A book club choice
text: In my [[opinion]], the mystery is a good choice for our reading group. I enjoy trying to solve a crime [[before]] the detective does. My friends [[agree]] with me: we all want to read it next. We plan to read the last chapter [[together]] on Friday, then choose [[another]] book.

title: Planning a field study
text: The [[purpose]] of the field study was to find out when birds used the pond. Before the first visit, the group agreed to [[collect]] data at fixed times each day. They tested the recording sheet [[before]] they began the main study. To make the results more [[reliable]], everyone used the same counting rules. Photographs provided [[evidence]] that the birds in the notes had been identified correctly.

title: A careful conclusion
text: [[Although]] litter counts fell after new signs were put up, the team did not immediately decide that the signs had caused the change. Fewer visitors might also have [[reduced]] the amount of rubbish. To test their [[claim]], they counted litter during busy weekends too. The lower counts continued. [[Therefore]], the council agreed to keep the signs in place for another [[month]].

title: Two ways to travel
text: A bicycle has the [[advantage]] of being cheap to use, while a bus can carry more people at once. One [[disadvantage]] of cycling is that rain makes the journey less comfortable. Adding a shelter had a noticeable [[effect]] on how dry passengers stayed at the bus stop. A second bus route could [[reduce]] delays, which would be a [[significant]] improvement for students who often arrived late.

title: Testing a source
text: A [[reliable]] report explains where its information came from, so readers can check it. In this survey, more than two hundred students answered questions about reading. [[However]], every response came from [[only]] one school. The researcher could not assume that those students would [[represent]] every teenager in the city. The answers provided useful [[evidence]] about reading habits at that school, with a clear limit on what could be concluded.

title: A story with a message
text: The filmmaker uses warm colours and lively music to [[create]] a hopeful mood. These choices encourage viewers to care about the main [[character]] as she tries to save her village. [[Although]] she has little money, she persuades her neighbours to work together. The final scene shows that small [[actions]] can make a difference. When the class meets afterwards, the teacher invites everyone to take part in a [[discussion]] about the ending.

title: Reading a campaign image
text: The campaign places two photographs side by side. One shows a crowded road, [[whereas]] the other presents the same space as a park. The caption adopts a calm [[tone]], inviting readers to consider the proposal rather than feel guilty about driving. Figures describing local pollution are directly [[relevant]] to residents deciding whether to support the plan. The argument is [[reinforced]] by a map linking the figures to particular streets. Viewers can therefore judge the proposal [[without]] having to guess whether the data describe their own neighbourhood.

title: A review with evidence
text: A strong [[analysis]] explains how a scene creates meaning rather than simply listing its events. In this review, the writer examines the director's decision to [[portray]] the young inventor as hesitant at first. Short answers reveal her discomfort, [[whereas]] longer speeches later suggest growing confidence. By looking [[closely]] at changes in her language, the reviewer connects an interpretation to details that can be checked. The argument becomes more [[convincing]] because each claim is supported by a specific moment from the film.

title: Designing a museum page
text: The museum page separates practical information from its illustrated exhibition guide. Clear [[navigation]] allows families to find opening times in a single click, [[whereas]] the exhibition section invites visitors to explore objects at a slower pace. A map is [[displayed]] beside the room descriptions, helping users understand how the galleries connect. Each object page can be reached [[without]] returning to the home screen. By explaining these routes [[clearly]], the design gives visitors control over their visit before they arrive at the building.

title: A balanced review
text: Short science videos [[tend to]] compress years of research into a single apparent breakthrough. This episode follows that familiar pattern; [[nevertheless]], it makes room for an interview with a researcher who questions the headline. The [[distinction]] between a promising early result and an established finding is explained through two contrasting examples. The limits of the evidence are [[acknowledged]] rather than hidden behind confident narration. Although the final claim still goes [[beyond]] what the small study can establish, the interview gives viewers grounds for questioning it.

title: The exhibition debate
text: To [[evaluate]] the exhibition fairly, students must consider how its claims are supported as well as which objects it contains. A useful starting point is the [[extent]] to which the labels distinguish established facts from disputed interpretations. The [[provenance]] of an object, or its recorded history of ownership, may explain why its presence in the collection is contested, [[although]] the display presents it as an uncomplicated national treasure. A judgement is better [[justified]] when it addresses that tension directly, drawing on both the curatorial language and the evidence supplied by the object itself rather than treating the label as a final authority.

title: A quiet scene
text: The untouched cup and [[unopened]] letter allow the reader to [[infer]] that an expected meeting has not taken place. Yet the passage never identifies the missing visitor. Its focus on [[absence]] makes the room seem shaped by what is not there, [[rather than]] by the furniture it contains. Details that might resolve the uncertainty are [[deliberately]] withheld: no date is given, and the envelope remains face down. This restraint lets the reader experience the character's waiting without supplying a confident explanation for it.

title: Whose story is centred?
text: Every documentary presents a [[perspective]], even when its narration adopts the language of neutrality. The editor determines [[whose]] experiences are included and which accounts remain outside the frame. If interviews are quoted [[selectively]], a disagreement that occupied most of a conversation can disappear behind a brief expression of support. The film may be [[explicit]] about when and where an event occurred while leaving the principles governing that selection unstated. Its apparent completeness therefore deserves scrutiny, [[because]] factual accuracy within individual statements does not guarantee a representative account of the wider event.

title: The lunch survey
text: Our class wanted to know which school lunch people liked best. We decided to [[ask]] everyone the same question [[before]] lunch. We wrote down the [[number]] of students who chose each meal. Then we counted the answers.

title: A clear sign
text: The new sign had a large red [[arrow]]. It pointed to the library door. The sign was [[easy]] to understand [[because]] it used a picture. Even children who could not read the words knew where to go.

title: Sorting the books
text: We put the animal books in one [[group]]. The books [[about]] sport went on a different shelf. We looked at the titles [[first]]. If a title was not clear, we opened the book and looked at the pictures.

title: Following the instructions
text: The card showed three simple [[steps]] for making a paper hat. We followed them in the right [[order]]. First we folded the paper. Then we folded it again. At the end, our hat was [[ready]] to wear.

title: The lost bag
text: Tom could not find his bag. He asked Mia [[where]] it was. She pointed at a chair. The bag was [[under]] it. Tom [[found]] his lunch box inside the bag and put it on the table.

title: A fair flight test
text: To compare two paper planes, we used the [[same]] type of paper for both. We [[measured]] how far each one flew. [[Before]] each flight, we stood on the same line. We wrote the [[results]] in a table. We checked that our numbers were [[accurate]] by measuring each distance twice. The longer plane flew further on all three attempts.

title: A change of route
text: The group took the river path [[instead of]] the main road. The teacher made this [[decision]] after checking the map. We could not use the road [[because]] workers had closed it. The path brought us [[closer]] to the museum, so everyone [[arrived]] before its doors opened.

title: An advert for the music club
text: The music club made an advert asking new students to [[join]] its weekly meetings. It used a [[large]] title so people could read it from across the hall. A line below explained [[when]] the meetings started. The [[information]] included the room number and the teacher's name. Students could find both details [[easily]] without asking anyone for help.

title: A useful photograph
text: Lena photographed her model [[while]] she was still at home. The picture would [[show]] what it looked like before the journey. On the bus, one of its legs was [[broken]] when her bag fell. In class, Lena used the photo as [[proof]] that she had finished the model. The teacher could see all four legs [[clearly]].

title: Two accounts of a trip
text: Two students wrote about the same school trip, but their accounts were [[different]]. One account was much longer, [[although]] both students had spent the same time writing. People often [[remember]] different parts of a shared day. We compared each [[description]] with the photos from the trip. [[Afterwards]], both writers added a detail that they had forgotten.

title: The missing survey replies
text: The [[purpose]] of the survey was to find out why some students stopped attending the homework club. Instead of asking only regular members, the organisers tried to [[collect]] replies from students who had left. They waited [[until]] the end of the week before adding up the answers. Several forms were still [[missing]], so the group explained this limit in its report. Readers could then judge the findings more [[carefully]], knowing whose views had been included.

title: Checking a rumour
text: A message claimed that the library would close for a month, but it named no [[source]]. Before sharing it, Priya [[spoke]] to the school librarian. Repairs were about to begin. [[However]], she explained that a [[single]] room would close, and students could still borrow books from the main desk. Priya posted the official notice so her friends could read the [[accurate]] information themselves. The original message had turned a small change into a much larger problem.

title: A plan for the team
text: Before the quiz, the team gave its members different [[roles]]. One person would read, another would write, and two would check the answers. [[Although]] everyone knew the topic, they had little time to practise together. They chose one shared sheet on which to [[record]] their answers. All four students had [[agreed]] to follow this plan. A clear division of work helped them finish before the [[deadline]].

title: Two headlines, one match
text: Two reports described the same football match. One headline called the result a lucky escape, [[whereas]] the other described it as a brave fightback. The first report [[emphasised]] the winners' mistakes; the second focused on their late goals. These choices could affect a reader's [[attitude]] towards the team. Someone reading either headline [[without]] the full report might imagine a different match. In fact, [[both]] reports gave the same score and described the same key events.

title: A quieter classroom
text: The teacher wanted to know whether a new carpet had any [[effect]] on classroom noise. She recorded sound levels for a week [[before]] it was fitted, then repeated the measurements. The class became [[noticeably]] quieter, but fewer students had attended during the second week. This difference placed a [[limit]] on what she could conclude. A fair [[comparison]] would require similar numbers of students in both weeks, as well as the same kind of lesson.

title: An impressive percentage
text: The article reports that half of the students surveyed prefer online lessons. That [[proportion]] sounds impressive, [[although]] the survey included only twenty students from one class. The researchers [[acknowledged]] that preferences might differ elsewhere, but they collected no replies from other schools. A headline presenting the result as the view of all teenagers would be [[misleading]], since the sample cannot support that claim. Readers should [[therefore]] examine who answered the survey before deciding how far the findings can be applied.

title: What the photograph leaves out
text: The published photograph shows a protester raising an arm, but the original frame included a child waving beside him. That surrounding detail has been [[omitted]], leaving readers with less [[context]] for judging the gesture. In the full image, the man's hand mirrors the child's, [[whereas]] the crop makes it seem directed at the police. The photograph is [[apparently]] a straightforward record of an angry protest, but a crop can [[distort]] the relationship between the people shown. The image remains genuine, yet the wider scene does not clearly support the interpretation encouraged by the crop.

title: Testing the ticket app
text: The design team assessed the app's [[usability]] by asking new users to book a ticket without guidance. A polished home screen counted for little [[unless]] participants could complete the task. When the back button led to different places, users became confused because it did not behave [[consistently]]. Their errors reflected a problem with the interface [[rather than]] a lack of interest in the event. The sessions [[revealed]] a difficulty that the designers, already familiar with every menu, had repeatedly overlooked. They changed the navigation before spending more time on the colours.

title: Distance and lateness
text: The report found a [[correlation]] between longer journeys and more frequent lateness. That pattern alone could not show that distance caused students to arrive late, [[because]] bus reliability and family routines might also influence the result. The team therefore examined each factor [[independently]] before combining the findings. A second survey could [[indicate]] whether the same relationship appeared in another year group. Even then, a [[causal]] explanation would require evidence about how the delays occurred, rather than a repeated association between two measurements.

title: Standards for a museum review
text: The reviewer set out clear [[criteria]] before visiting the exhibition: readable labels, a coherent route and a range of perspectives. The route was easy to follow [[despite]] the building's awkward shape. Labels beside the main objects were [[accessible]] to younger visitors, with difficult terms explained in ordinary language. To [[justify]] a positive judgement, however, the review also needed to consider the neglected side rooms. Applying the same standards [[consistently]] would prevent the most attractive gallery from standing in for the quality of the exhibition as a whole.

title: Before does not mean because
text: The council's [[attribution]] of falling traffic levels to its new cycle scheme is premature. Although the scheme [[preceded]] the decline, the same period also saw the closure of a major office complex. A sequence of events does not [[necessarily]] establish a cause, particularly when another change offers a [[plausible]] explanation for the outcome. [[Unless]] the report distinguishes the influence of those competing factors, its confident claim exceeds what the figures can demonstrate. A comparison with streets unaffected by either change might sharpen the analysis, though differences between those areas would still need to be considered.

title: The silences in an archive
text: An archive can be extensive and still offer a [[selective]] record of the past. Its contents depend partly on what the collecting [[institution]] considered worth preserving. If official correspondence was retained [[systematically]] while informal testimony was discarded, the collection will give unequal visibility to different experiences. Surviving documents may reveal policy in considerable detail, [[whereas]] the responses of those affected remain difficult to recover. The resulting [[silence]] should not be treated as proof that such responses never existed. It is a feature of the surviving evidence, requiring explanation rather than an invitation to fill the gap with unsupported certainty.

title: The boundaries of a claim
text: The author's conclusion is carefully [[qualified]]: the proposed explanation applies to the communities studied, and only during the period for which records survive. This gives the argument a clearly defined [[scope]] rather than exposing a flaw in it. A critic cannot refute the claim [[merely]] by identifying a different pattern elsewhere, since that evidence falls [[beyond]] the stated boundary. To challenge the conclusion, the critic would need to show that it is contradicted by [[evidence]] from the cases the author actually examines. Precision about limits makes the disagreement more productive by establishing what each side would have to demonstrate.

title: Translating a narrator's voice
text: The translation preserves the narrator's formal [[register]], even when a more conversational phrase would sound smoother in English. The narrator's politeness is not a sign of friendliness, [[although]] the courteous phrases might initially suggest otherwise. By carrying that pattern through [[consistently]], the translator allows readers to detect the tension between courteous language and unfriendly conduct. The translator avoids [[flattening]] the narrator's voice into ordinary conversation, even at the cost of perfect fluency. A wholly [[literal]] version could preserve the dictionary meaning of individual phrases while losing the pattern of evasion that makes those phrases significant in the first place.

title: A report and its sponsor
text: The report's [[disclosure]] of its funding source helps readers judge a possible conflict of interest, [[although]] transparency alone does not establish that the analysis is sound. What matters next is whether the data can be examined [[independently]] and whether the stated method accounts for inconvenient findings as well as favourable ones. Readers should neither [[assume]] that sponsorship invalidates the work nor accept its conclusions solely because the sponsor has been named. The relevant safeguards are [[procedural]]: access to the underlying evidence, a method open to scrutiny and a clear explanation of how competing interpretations were assessed.
